data.text/markdown:
Oracle Audit

Two families of in-silico AMP oracles disagree in sign about which peptides are antimicrobial. Pick one and watch it happen — then audit your own peptide against the mechanism.

Generative antimicrobial-peptide (AMP) design is scored almost entirely by in-silico oracles — published sequence classifiers that return "probability of being an AMP". Nobody wet-labs a million candidates, so the oracle is the benchmark. This notebook audits the benchmark itself. The test is deliberately blunt. Take three cohorts whose labels nobody disputes:
  • real AMPs — 2,000 curated, experimentally validated antimicrobials,
  • shuffled decoys — the same 2,000 peptides with their residues permuted, so amino-acid composition, length and net charge are preserved and only the sequence order is destroyed,
  • curated non-AMPs — 877 peptides annotated as non-antimicrobial.
A usable oracle must rank real AMPs above both. Several widely cited ones do the opposite: they flag 87.5% of composition-matched shuffles and 66.8% of real AMPs. Design pipelines then select tens of thousands of sequences on exactly that signal.
How to read this Nothing here is a screenshot. Every panel recomputes in your browser — 4,977 peptides x 16 oracles for the audit, plus an in-browser peptide analyser, an order-2 Markov decoy generator and a 21-feature composition oracle that you can point at any sequence you paste in. Sections. 0 — the audit (pick an oracle, move the threshold). 1 — audit any peptide, with helical wheels and a 3D helix. 2 — generate decoys that fool the oracle. 3 — why the published oracles behave this way.
0. The audit — pick an oracle, move the threshold

0.1 Where the three cohorts land

If the oracle encodes antimicrobial function, the green distribution (real AMPs) sits to the right of the pink one (its own shuffled decoys). If it encodes composition only, the two distributions collapse onto each other — and in the Family-B oracles the shuffles land to the right.

0.2 The panel that matters: precision vs selection depth

Both families look fine at the top of a ranked list — the published papers report precision@100, and at k=100 precision is 0.92 (amPEPpy), 0.90 (AMPlify) and 1.00 (OmegAMP broad). Real design pipelines do not stop at 100. The curve below screens real AMPs out of a 50/50 pool against their own shuffled decoys: rank the 4,000 peptides by the selected oracle, descending, and plot precision@k. The marker is the depth at which precision first falls below 0.75 — the point past which the oracle is no longer separating function from composition. It arrives at k=265 for amPEPpy and k=240 for AMPlify but not until k=691 for the OmegAMP broad classifier: a 2.6x difference in usable selection depth, which is the whole audit in one number.

data.text/markdown:
1. Audit any peptide

Paste a sequence, or draw one from the audit cohorts. Everything below is computed in your browser from the sequence string alone. The two helical wheels are the scientific heart of this notebook. They show the same residues — identical composition, identical length, identical net charge — arranged in the real order and in a permuted order. An ideal alpha-helix advances 100 deg per residue, so order decides which residues share a face. The real AMP usually shows a contiguous hydrophobic arc (shaded wedge, arrow = hydrophobic moment direction); its shuffle usually does not. A composition-only oracle sees nothing to distinguish them, and that is the whole mechanism behind the sign inversion above.

data.text/markdown:
1.1 The same peptide as a 3D helix

An idealised alpha-helix built analytically from the sequence — CA on a helix of radius 2.3 A, rise 1.5 A per residue, 100 deg per residue, with CB projected outward (glycine omitted). Residues are coloured by Eisenberg hydrophobicity (red = hydrophobic, blue = charged/polar), so the amphipathic stripe that the wheel shows as a wedge appears in 3D as a coloured face running up one side of the cylinder. Drag to rotate. This is a geometric idealisation, not a structure prediction — no folding is implied.

data.text/markdown:
2. Generate decoys that fool the oracle

An order-2 Markov chain fitted to the 2,000 curated real AMPs (transition counts embedded above; ^^ is the start context). It reproduces local residue statistics and nothing else — no helix, no amphipathicity, no function. Sample from it, score every sample with the composition-only oracle, and count how many a published composition-driven classifier would call antimicrobial.

data.text/html: These 200 sequences were drawn from residue statistics alone. They have no designed helix and no amphipathic face, yet 118 of them clear the threshold that the published composition-driven oracle uses to declare a peptide antimicrobial — against 62.3% of experimentally validated AMPs. That is what a generative pipeline optimising such an oracle is free to exploit.
The generated set, ranked by the oracle it is fooling (paste any row into section 1 to see its wheel):

data.text/markdown:
3. Why the published oracles behave this way

Fit a 21-feature logistic regression — the 20 amino-acid frequencies plus length/50, no order information whatsoever — to predict amPEPpy's own binary call. If amPEPpy were reading function, a bag-of-residues model should fail.

data.text/markdown:
Data provenance

Every number above is recomputed in-browser. The audit panels run from per-peptide oracle scores embedded in this notebook (gzip + base64, ~260 kB); the explorer panels run from a second embedded blob (~0.2 MB of JSON) holding the Markov transition counts, the composition-oracle weights, the mimic scatter and the headline statistics. The published build therefore fetches no data at runtime and needs no server and no login. The one external resource is the 3Dmol.js bundle in section 1.1, loaded from a CDN; if it is unavailable the viewer says so and the helical wheels carry the same information.
  • Peptides — 4,977 sequences: 2,000 curated real AMPs, 2,000 composition-preserving shuffles of those same AMPs (residue permutation preserves length, composition and net charge), 877 curated non-AMPs, and the 100 sequences of a real competition submission.
  • Family A oracles (13) — OmegAMP's hard-negative-trained classifiers: the broad classifier, 5 per-species and 7 per-strain heads. Scored probabilities.
  • Family B oracles (3) — amPEPpy, AMPlify (probabilities) and AMPredictor (predicted MIC in uM, lower = more active; thresholded at the MIC cutoff slider, default 16 uM).
  • Derived live — positive rates at the chosen decision rule, precision@k on the 50/50 real-AMP vs shuffled-decoy pool, k* (the depth at which precision@k first drops below 0.75, k >= 20), peptide net charge / mean hydrophobicity / hydrophobic moment, helical wheels, the idealised helix coordinates, the composition-oracle score, and the order-2 Markov samples.
  • Scales — Eisenberg consensus hydrophobicity; mu_H computed at 100 deg per residue and normalised by length; net charge at pH 7 with K,R = +1, D,E = -1, H = +0.1.
Part of Oracle Audit, an OSI Hackathon 2026 submission: a benchmark-validity audit of the in-silico oracles used to evaluate generative AMP design.
